doc.title: Jon Weber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 2, 2012

title: Quoting other songs: spare parts and Teddy Wilson
summary: Rowe noticed a Frankie and Johnny quote; Weber explains spare parts, quoting, and playful off-key quotes with John Faushager.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I was listening to you play “Green Dolphin Street” and I heard you play “Frankie and Johnny.”

Yeah really. I knew you were going to say that, or I thought you would. “Really?” Like it almost was so subtly done, but I’m pretty sure it was, but I remember at the moment listening to it. I wonder if you knew that you did that or if it was just so — it was a half a quote almost.
I think I remember the venue. I think it was The Artist’s Corner in Minneapolis and you probably saw it on YouTube maybe? Alex Hahn on alto sax?

An alto sax player kid, he’s about 24. Unbelievable. I did a gig with him when he was 17. In any case yeah, the spare parts. Teddy Wilson, the great pianist whose centennial is this year on the 24th of November, 1912, he used to call them “spare parts.” Where you’d be playing a song and all of a sudden you’d hear [scats] and it’s sneaking in there. It’s a joke. It’s a little jest. It’s a little sneaky thing that, it fits. Some people force/impose them and go out of their way to put in something silly.

Especially at Christmastime, right. Oh this is a good 35 Christmas carols. If I hear somebody play a spare part of a song, like “Frankie and Johnny,” if there’s a bridge, I © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

will try to answer that person by doing a quote from the bridge. That’s my drill. But the spare parts. I love it. That’s, to me, when somebody does that, when someone takes a snip of another song and puts it in on the fly in real time into the song, and then goes back to what they were doing — oh where was I — that’s a pretty high level of human expression if you think about it. They were already improvising over chords, a new melody in real time, not the slow motion composition. You know Wayne Shorter said something about composition is improvising in slow motion and improvising is composition in fast motion or real time, which I love. But they’re on the fly improvising something and then taking a snip of another song — oh I think I’ll take this one out of orbit for a second and put it in, and, no, put it back.
Right. Because you have to know what pitch that quote starts on too, right. You can’t just like — unless you’re doing it out of key on purpose or something.

Well that used to happen a lot. I remember I had a gig with a gentleman named John Faushager and we used to quote things like “Daniel Boone” — something that didn’t have any business being in there, and we’d make it off key to see if we could even turn their head after a while, “Don’t you hear that?” We’ll make is a flat nine and see.
